This page builds every variable used in the analysis, one step at a time,
starting from the children's decisions in the game and their answers to the
nomination survey:

| Step | Measure | What it captures |
|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | Cooperation GAP | who came out ahead in a pair's exchange |
| 3 | Friendship type | whether the two children named each other as best friends |
| 4 | Social Rank | each child's standing in the classroom, from popularity nominations |
| 5 | Social Rank GAP | the rank difference between the two children of a pair |
| 6 | Null-model filter | a robustness check that keeps the most partner-specific transfers |

The code shown here is the code in `code/01_build_measures.R`: the page reads
it chunk by chunk (with `knitr::read_chunk`), so the script and the page can
never drift apart. Running this page also writes the two files used by the
[main results](02_main_results.qmd).

# The data

The experiment took place in 45 classrooms. In each classroom, children were
paired with every classmate once, across several rounds. In each pair, the
child received 10 tokens and decided how many to give to the partner (tokens
given were doubled for the receiver). After the game, each child answered
nine peer-nomination questions (name 2 to 5 classmates who...).

There are two files:

- `data/raw/dyads.csv`: one row per **decision**, sender $i$ → receiver $j$. It has
  the tokens $i$ sent to $j$, the round, and nine 0/1 columns `nom_q1` to
  `nom_q9` that say whether $i$ named $j$ in each question.
- `data/raw/students.csv`: one row per child, with sex, age, GPA and attendance.

The data use study codes. Variable definitions are in `data/codebook.md`.


# Step 1. Tokens received

A decision tells us what $i$ sent to $j$. What $i$ *received* from $j$ is
$j$'s decision toward $i$, which is another row of the same file. We find it
by swapping sender and receiver and joining.

```{r tokens-received}
```

Both decisions of a pair are always in the same round: each pair of
classmates played together once, and in that round each one decided for the
other. We can also check directly that no pair played more than once:

```{r}
dyads %>%
  mutate(child_a = pmin(sender_id, receiver_id),
         child_b = pmax(sender_id, receiver_id)) %>%
  group_by(child_a, child_b) %>%
  summarise(rounds = n_distinct(round), decisions = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  count(rounds, decisions)
```

8,902 pairs, each with two decisions in a single round.

# Step 2. Cooperation GAP

$$
\text{Coop GAP}_{ij} = w_{ji} - w_{ij} \quad \text{(tokens received minus tokens sent)}
$$

```{r cooperation-gap}
```

```{r}
summary(dyads$coop_gap)
```

The Cooperation GAP of $j \to i$ is the Cooperation GAP of $i \to j$ with the
opposite sign, so it averages exactly zero over the whole sample. What
matters is not its level but *who* ends up ahead: the analysis asks whether
the child who comes out ahead tends to be the higher-ranked one.

# Step 3. Friendship type

Question 3 asked for the child's **best friends**. A pair is *mutual* if both
named each other, *one-sided* if only one did, and *non-friends* if neither
did. For one-sided pairs we keep track of who named whom.

```{r friendship-type}
```

Each one-sided pair appears twice: once as "Sender declares" (seen from the
child who named the other) and once as "Receiver declares" (seen from the
other child). Together they are the 14.6% of asymmetric friendships.

# Step 4. Social Rank

Social Rank comes from questions 4 (*most popular and well-known*) and 5
(*not popular or well-known*). We combine them in one network per classroom,
where the edge $i \to j$ has weight

$$
a_{ij} = P^+_{ij} - P^-_{ij} + 1 \in \{0, 1, 2\}.
$$

```{r popularity-network}
```

The $+1$ keeps every weight non-negative, as PageRank requires: a
popularity nomination gives weight 2, no nomination weight 1, and a
non-popularity nomination weight 0.

Why PageRank rather than a simple count of nominations? PageRank gives more
weight to nominations that come from children who are themselves highly
regarded, in the same way that a web page linked by important pages is
important. A child named as popular by well-regarded classmates ranks higher
than one named by classmates whom few regard as popular.

We compute PageRank in each classroom and rescale it from 0 (lowest in the
class) to 1 (highest in the class), so that ranks are comparable across
classrooms of different size.

```{r pagerank}
```

As an illustration, the ranks in the small classroom used in Figure 2:

```{r}
students %>%
  filter(class_id == 16) %>%
  select(student_id, female, pagerank, social_rank) %>%
  arrange(desc(social_rank))
```

# Step 5. Social Rank GAP

$$
\text{RankGAP}_{ij} = \text{Rank}_i - \text{Rank}_j
$$

Positive values mean the sender has the higher rank. Since both ranks run
from 0 to 1 within a classroom, the gap runs from $-1$ (the lowest-ranked
child meets the highest-ranked one) to $1$ (the reverse). Most pairs are
much closer: 83% of the decisions have a gap between $-0.5$ and $0.5$.

```{r rank-gap}
```

:::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

```{r}
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = "grey60", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Social Rank GAP", y = "Decisions") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Step 6. Student covariates

Some analyses use student characteristics: attendance, GPA and age, and the
nominations each child received in each peer question. All of them are
standardized here, within each classroom (mean 0 and SD 1 among
classmates), so a value compares a child with her own classmates and not with
children of other schools. The z-scores are saved in
`analysis_students.csv`, and every script reads them from there.

- `attendance_z` enters the balance check (Figure 1D, Table S16, Figures
  S15–S17). GPA enters that check on its original 1–7 scale, as in the
  paper.
- The other z-scores are used in the correlates of Social Rank (Table S9,
  Figure S8) and of Behavioral Social Rank (Figure S30).
- The two computed ages above 15 years are birth-date errors (SI Table S1)
  and are set to missing before standardizing.

```{r student-covariates}
```

# Step 7. Null-model filtering (robustness)

Some children give 5 tokens to everyone; others give 10 to some classmates
and 0 to others. Only the second kind of giving says something about the
partner. The filtered analysis asks whether the rank pattern is still there
when we look only at the transfers that depart most from each child's usual
way of giving. It is a robustness check: the main regressions already absorb
each child's average generosity with sender fixed effects.

The null model shuffles, for each sender, *who* receives each of her
allocations, keeping the allocations themselves. Under this shuffle the
expected value and the standard deviation of any cell $i \to j$ are just the
mean and the standard deviation of the sender's own allocations. Each
transfer is scored by

$$
d_{ij} = \frac{|w_{ij} - \bar{w}_i|}{\text{SD}(w_i)}.
$$

```{r null-model-score}
```

**Check with actual shuffles.** The SI describes the null model with 1,000
random shuffles. Here we do them for one classroom and compare the
simulated mean and standard deviation of each cell with the closed form
used above.

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
one_class <- dyads %>% filter(class_id == 16)

simulated <- one_class %>%
  group_by(sender_id) %>%
  group_modify(function(rows, key) {
    shuffles <- replicate(1000, sample(rows$tokens_sent))   # one column per shuffle
    tibble(receiver_id = rows$receiver_id,
           tokens_sent = rows$tokens_sent,
           mean_sim    = rowMeans(shuffles),
           sd_sim      = apply(shuffles, 1, function(x) sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2))))
  }) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  left_join(one_class %>% select(sender_id, receiver_id, sender_mean, sender_sd),
            by = c("sender_id", "receiver_id"))

simulated %>%
  summarise(max_difference_mean = max(abs(mean_sim - sender_mean)),
            max_difference_sd   = max(abs(sd_sim - sender_sd)))
```

The differences are of the size expected from 1,000 random draws (they get
smaller as the number of shuffles grows). The closed form is the exact limit of the simulation, so we use it: same scores, and no randomness in the
results.

Then we keep the 50% of transfers with the highest score (one cutoff for the whole sample). A pair enters the filtered Cooperation GAP only if *both*
directions are kept, so about a quarter of the pairs remain.

```{r null-model-filter}
```
